tips.title: The index counts the copies
tips.body: $5^3$ means $5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$, not $5 \times 3$. The index says **how many copies are multiplied**, not what to multiply by.

tips.title: Brackets decide where the minus goes
tips.body: $(-4)^2 = 16$ but $-4^2 = -16$. Without a bracket the power applies to the 4 only and the minus stays outside. Always read the brackets before evaluating.

tips.title: Even roots of negatives do not exist
tips.body: A negative number has no real square root, because anything squared is positive. It does have a **cube** root: $\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2$. Odd roots are fine, even roots are not.

steps.title: Squares, cubes, and the roots that undo them
steps.body:
A **power** tells you how many copies of a number to multiply together. $7^2 = 7 \times 7 = 49$ is *7 squared*; $4^3 = 4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$ is *4 cubed*.

A **root** runs the machine backwards. $\sqrt{49} = 7$ asks *what squares to 49*, and $\sqrt[3]{64} = 4$ asks *what cubes to 64*.

The single trap here catches people every year: $5^3$ is $125$, not $15$. The small number counts the copies, it is not something to multiply by.

visuals.alt: Three boxes each holding a 4, multiplied together to give 64

check.solution: $4^2 = 4 \times 4 = 16$. The answer $8$ comes from doing $4 \times 2$ instead.

steps.title: Roots above the third
steps.body:
Squaring and cubing are just the first two rungs. You can go as high as you like, and every power has a matching root.

$2^4 = 16$, so $\sqrt[4]{16} = 2$. $3^5 = 243$, so $\sqrt[5]{243} = 3$.

The small number sitting in the crook of the root sign is the **index** of the root. A square root is the only one that leaves it out: $\sqrt{25}$ means $\sqrt[2]{25}$.

Worth knowing by heart: the powers of 2 up to $2^{10} = 1024$, and the squares up to $15^2 = 225$. They come up constantly and save you minutes in a non-calculator paper.

visuals.alt: Five boxes each holding a 2, multiplied together to give 32

steps.text: Ask: what number multiplied by itself five times gives 32?
steps.note: the 5 in the crook says five copies
build up in stages rather than guessing

steps.title: Where the minus sign sits
steps.body:
These two look almost the same and mean different things:

$$(-3)^2 = (-3) \times (-3) = 9 \qquad -3^2 = -(3 \times 3) = -9$$

The bracket decides. With a bracket, the minus is **inside** and gets squared away. Without one, the power happens first and the minus is left sitting in front.

The general rule for a negative number raised to a power: an **even** power gives a positive answer, because the minus signs pair up and cancel. An **odd** power leaves one minus over, so the answer is negative.

$(-2)^4 = 16$ but $(-2)^3 = -8$.

steps.text: $(-3)^2$: the bracket holds the minus, so it is $(-3) \times (-3)$
$-3^2$: no bracket, so square the 3 first
$3^2 = 9$, and the minus stays in front: $= -9$

check.solution: The bracket squares the whole of $-6$: $(-6) \times (-6) = 36$.

steps.title: Roots of negative numbers
steps.body:
Cube roots of negatives are fine. $(-5)^3 = -125$, so $\sqrt[3]{-125} = -5$. Any **odd** root of a negative number is negative.

Square roots of negatives are a different story. Nothing you square gives a negative answer, because positive $\times$ positive and negative $\times$ negative are both positive. So $\sqrt{-9}$ has no value among the numbers you use at GCSE. If a calculation hands you a square root of a negative, you have made a slip somewhere.

One more piece of notation to be exact about: the sign $\sqrt{\ }$ means the **positive** root only. Both $7$ and $-7$ square to $49$, but $\sqrt{49}$ is $7$. The two-sign version has to be written out, as $\pm\sqrt{49}$, and you will need it when you solve $x^2 = 49$.

visuals.problem: Which of these have a value?

steps.text: $\sqrt{-16}$: no value at GCSE, since nothing squared is negative

steps.note: $x^2 = 16$ has two answers; $\sqrt{16}$ is one number

check.prompt: Which of these has no value at GCSE?
check.solution: Odd roots of negatives are fine, and $\sqrt{0} = 0$. Only the square root of a negative has no value, because no number squared is negative.

steps.title: Fractions and decimals
steps.body:
For a fraction, deal with the top and the bottom separately:

$$\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 = \dfrac{3^2}{4^2} = \dfrac{9}{16} \qquad \sqrt{\dfrac{25}{36}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{25}}{\sqrt{36}} = \dfrac{5}{6}$$

Decimals are where people go wrong, because the answer moves in a way that feels backwards. $\sqrt{0.04} = 0.2$, not $0.02$. The reliable check is to square your answer and see whether you get back where you started: $0.2 \times 0.2 = 0.04$, so it is right, while $0.02 \times 0.02 = 0.0004$, so it is not.

And notice that a root of a number between 0 and 1 comes out **larger** than the number you started with. $\sqrt{0.25} = 0.5$, and $0.5 > 0.25$.

steps.note: Turning the decimal into a fraction removes the guesswork

steps.title: Reciprocals, and what a negative power means
steps.body:
The **reciprocal** of a number is 1 divided by it. The reciprocal of $5$ is $\dfrac{1}{5}$, and the reciprocal of $\dfrac{2}{3}$ is $\dfrac{3}{2}$: for a fraction you simply turn it upside down.

A number times its reciprocal is always $1$, which is the whole point of it.

This is what a negative index is doing. Going down the ladder of powers, each step divides by the base, and the pattern does not stop when you reach $2^0 = 1$:

$$2^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2} \qquad 2^{-3} = \dfrac{1}{2^3} = \dfrac{1}{8}$$

So $a^{-1}$ is exactly the reciprocal of $a$. A negative index never makes the answer negative; it flips it.

visuals.alt: Powers of 2 from 2 cubed down to 2 to the minus 2, each rung dividing by 2

steps.note: a decimal is hard to flip; a fraction is easy

check.prompt: Work out $3^{-2}$. Give your answer as a fraction.
check.solution: $3^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{3^2} = \dfrac{1}{9} = 0.111\ldots$ The answer is positive: a negative index flips, it does not make things negative.

steps.title: Estimating a root that is not exact
steps.body:
Most roots are not whole numbers, and a non-calculator paper will ask you to trap one between the two whole numbers either side.

The method is always the same: find the squares just **below** and just **above** the number.

For $\sqrt{50}$: $7^2 = 49$ and $8^2 = 64$. Since $49 < 50 < 64$, the root sits between $7$ and $8$. It is only just above 49, so $\sqrt{50}$ is barely above $7$.

This works because squaring keeps positive numbers in order: if one number is bigger than another, so is its square. That is the sentence that earns the mark in a *show that* question.

visuals.alt: A number line from 6 to 9 with the root of 50 marked just above 7, and 7 squared is 49 and 8 squared is 64 labelled beneath

visuals.problem: $\sqrt[3]{100}$ lies between two consecutive whole numbers. Find them.

steps.note: cube root, so use cubes, not squares
this line is the mark in a show-that question
nearer 5, since 100 is closer to 125 than to 64

check.prompt: $\sqrt{30}$ lies between two consecutive whole numbers. Write down the smaller one.
check.solution: $5^2 = 25$ and $6^2 = 36$. Since $25 < 30 < 36$, the root is between $5$ and $6$.

steps.title: Powers and roots inside a bigger calculation
steps.body:
In the order of operations, powers and roots are settled **before** any multiplying, dividing, adding or subtracting, and **after** anything inside brackets.

A root sign also acts as a bracket: everything underneath it is worked out first. In $\sqrt{9 + 16}$ you add before you root, giving $\sqrt{25} = 5$, which is not the same as $\sqrt{9} + \sqrt{16} = 7$.

steps.text: Now the power and the root: $3^2 = 9$ and $\sqrt{25} = 5$

steps.note: Doing $2 \times 3$ first would give 36 − 5, and the wrong answer

steps.text: $5 \neq 7$, so roots cannot be split across a $+$
steps.note: The same is true of a $-$

check.skill: order of operations with powers and roots
check.solution: Power and root first: $2^3 = 8$ and $\sqrt{81} = 9$. Then $5 \times 8 = 40$, and $40 + 9 = 49$.

steps.title: Your turn: work down to the value
steps.body:
Work out $\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{-2}$ one line at a time.

Two ideas meet here: a negative index means take the reciprocal, and a power of a fraction goes to the top and the bottom separately. Do the flip first and the rest is a square you already know.

visuals.fallback: A negative index flips the fraction: $\left(\tfrac{2}{3}\right)^{-2} = \left(\tfrac{3}{2}\right)^{2}$. Squaring the top and the bottom gives $\tfrac{9}{4}$, which is $2.25$.

check.prompt: Work out $\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^{-2}$. Give your answer as a fraction.
check.solution: Flip for the negative index: $\left(\tfrac{5}{3}\right)^2$. Then square top and bottom: $\tfrac{25}{9}$.

steps.title: Going deeper: judging size without working it out
steps.body:
Grade 9 questions rarely ask you to evaluate something; they ask you to **compare** or to **justify**.

*Which is larger, $2^{10}$ or $10^3$?* The base 10 is bigger, so it feels as though $10^3$ should win. It does not. $2^{10} = 1024$ and $10^3 = 1000$. The index matters as much as the base, and the only safe move is to work both out.

*Is $\sqrt{0.5}$ bigger or smaller than $0.5$?* Bigger. Squaring a number between 0 and 1 makes it smaller, so rooting one makes it larger. $\sqrt{0.5} \approx 0.71$.

*Show that $\sqrt{40}$ is between 6 and 7.* The marks are for $6^2 = 36$, $7^2 = 49$, and $36 < 40 < 49$ written down. Writing $\sqrt{40} = 6.32\ldots$ scores nothing: a *show that* question wants the reasoning, not the number.

steps.text: Do not compare the bases or the indices on their own; they point opposite ways

steps.note: The bigger index beat the bigger base here, but it does not always

check.prompt: Which of these statements is true?
check.solution: $\sqrt{0.16} = 0.4$, and $0.4 > 0.16$. Rooting a number between 0 and 1 always makes it larger.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **A power counts copies**: $5^3 = 5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$, never $5 \times 3$.
- **A root undoes a power**: $\sqrt[3]{125} = 5$. The index in the crook says which power it undoes.
- **Brackets decide the sign**: $(-3)^2 = 9$ but $-3^2 = -9$.
- **Even powers of negatives are positive, odd powers are negative**: $(-2)^4 = 16$, $(-2)^3 = -8$.
- **Odd roots of negatives exist, square roots of negatives do not**: $\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2$, but $\sqrt{-8}$ has no value at GCSE.
- **The sign $\sqrt{\ }$ means the positive root only**: $\sqrt{49} = 7$, while $x^2 = 49$ gives $x = \pm 7$.
- **Fractions split top and bottom**: $\sqrt{\tfrac{25}{36}} = \tfrac{5}{6}$. For decimals, turn them into fractions and check by squaring back.
- **A negative index flips**: $a^{-1}$ is the reciprocal of $a$, and $2^{-3} = \tfrac{1}{8}$. It never makes the answer negative.
- **To estimate a root**, name the squares either side: $49 < 50 < 64$, so $7 < \sqrt{50} < 8$. Those three statements are the marks.

visuals.alt: A card of the five index laws with one example each

questions.solution: $5^3$ means $5 \times 5 \times 5 = 125$. It does not mean $5 \times 3$; that would give 15.
$4 \times 4 \times 4 = 64$, so $\sqrt[3]{64} = 4$. Do not confuse it with $\sqrt{64} = 8$.

questions.prompt: Which of these is equal to $2^5$?
questions.solution: $2^5 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 32$. $2 \times 5 = 10$ and $2^4 = 16$ are the two usual slips.
The bracket means the whole of $-4$ is squared: $(-4) \times (-4) = 16$. A negative times a negative is positive.
With no bracket, the power is applied first and the minus sign stays outside: $-(5^2) = -25$. Compare $(-5)^2 = 25$.

markScheme.description: squares first, keeping the minus sign outside

questions.prompt: Work out $\left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)^3$. Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.solution: Raise the top and the bottom separately: $2^3 = 8$ and $5^3 = 125$, so the answer is $\dfrac{8}{125}$.

questions.prompt: Work out $\sqrt{\dfrac{49}{4}}$. Give your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: Root the top and the bottom separately: $\sqrt{49} = 7$ and $\sqrt{4} = 2$, so the answer is $\dfrac{7}{2} = 3.5$.

questions.prompt: Write down the reciprocal of $8$. Give your answer as a decimal.
questions.solution: The reciprocal of $8$ is $\dfrac{1}{8} = 0.125$. In index form that is $8^{-1}$.

questions.skill: order of operations with powers and roots
questions.solution: Powers and roots come before adding: $9 + 4 = 13$.

questions.prompt: $\sqrt{150}$ lies between two consecutive whole numbers. Write down the smaller one.
questions.solution: $12^2 = 144$ and $13^2 = 169$. Since $144 < 150 < 169$, $\sqrt{150}$ lies between $12$ and $13$, so the smaller is $12$.
A cube root of a negative number is negative: $(-5)^3 = -125$, so $\sqrt[3]{-125} = -5$. The $\sqrt{\ }$ sign means the positive root, so $\sqrt{121} = 11$. Then $-5 + 11 = 6$.
An even power of a negative is positive: $(-2)^4 = 16$. An odd power stays negative: $(-2)^3 = -8$. Subtracting a negative adds: $16 - (-8) = 24$.
Ask what squares to $0.04$. $0.2 \times 0.2 = 0.04$, so the answer is $0.2$. The common wrong answer is $0.02$; check it by squaring, since $0.02^2 = 0.0004$.
Squaring loses the sign, so there are two numbers whose square is $\tfrac{1}{16}$: $n = \tfrac{1}{4}$ or $n = -\tfrac{1}{4}$. The condition $n < 0$ picks the negative one: $n = -0.25$.

questions.prompt: A square has an area of $90$ cm². Its side length lies between two consecutive whole numbers of centimetres. Write down the larger one.
questions.solution: The side length is $\sqrt{90}$. $9^2 = 81$ and $10^2 = 100$, and $81 < 90 < 100$, so the side is between $9$ cm and $10$ cm. The larger is $10$.

questions.prompt: Show that $\sqrt{40}$ lies between $6$ and $7$. You must not use a calculator.
questions.solution: Square both ends of the claimed range and show 40 sits inside it. $6^2 = 36$, $7^2 = 49$, and $36 < 40 < 49$. Because squaring keeps positive numbers in order, taking the square root of all three gives $6 < \sqrt{40} < 7$. A bare statement that $\sqrt{40} \approx 6.3$ scores nothing in a show-that question: the squares have to be on the page.

criteria.text: The conclusion $6 < \sqrt{40} < 7$ is drawn from the comparison, not just asserted

questions.modelAnswer: $6^2 = 36$ and $7^2 = 49$. Since $36 < 40 < 49$, and squaring keeps positive numbers in the same order, $\sqrt{36} < \sqrt{40} < \sqrt{49}$, that is $6 < \sqrt{40} < 7$, as required.

questions.prompt: Without a calculator, decide which is larger: $2^{10}$ or $10^3$. Show how you know.
questions.solution: Work both out. $2^{10} = 1024$, either by doubling ten times or as $(2^5)^2 = 32^2 = 1024$. $10^3 = 1000$. So $2^{10}$ is larger, by 24. Saying '10 is bigger than 3 so $10^3$ wins' compares the wrong parts; the base and the index both matter.

markScheme.description: $2^{10}$ evaluated, or a valid route such as $(2^5)^2$

criteria.text: The two are compared and $2^{10}$ named as the larger

examTechnique.body:
Powers and roots turn up as one-mark starters and as the first line of much longer questions, so a slip here costs marks a long way downstream. Almost every mark lost is one of four things: reading $5^3$ as $5 \times 3$, losing a minus sign, splitting a root across a plus, or quoting a decimal when the question said *show that*.

On a non-calculator paper, knowing the squares to $15^2$ and the powers of 2 to $2^{10}$ is worth real time. On a calculator paper, still write the squares down in an estimating question: the marks are for the reasoning.
examinerErrors: Evaluating $5^3$ as $15$. The index counts how many copies to multiply, it is not a multiplier.
Writing $-4^2 = 16$. Without a bracket the power is applied first and the minus stays outside, so it is $-16$. Only $(-4)^2$ is $16$.
Giving $\sqrt{0.04}$ as $0.02$. Squaring the answer back is the check: $0.02^2 = 0.0004$, so it cannot be right.
Splitting a root across an addition: $\sqrt{9 + 16}$ is $5$, not $3 + 4$. The root sign acts as a bracket.
Answering a *show that* estimating question with a calculator decimal. The marks are for the two squares and the comparison between them, not for the value.
Treating $\sqrt{49}$ as $\pm 7$. The sign means the positive root; the $\pm$ appears only when you solve $x^2 = 49$.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer writes the reasoning down rather than the result. Asked to estimate $\sqrt{40}$, it puts $6^2 = 36$ and $7^2 = 49$ on the page, states $36 < 40 < 49$, and concludes $6 < \sqrt{40} < 7$ from that comparison. Asked which of two powers is larger, it evaluates both instead of comparing bases or indices on their own. It keeps signs under control without thinking about it, knowing an even power of a negative is positive and an odd one is negative, and it checks any decimal root by squaring it back.
